checked.note: Verbatim: 'he ended up with more equations than there were unknowns.' Page attributes this to Legendre's comet-orbit work; narration 'you get more equations than unknowns' is supported.
Verbatim: 'In an appendix Legendre gave the least squares method of fitting a curve to the data available.' Supports narration 'Legendre published the fix first.'

Verbatim: 'while acknowledging that it appeared in Legendre's book, Gauss still claimed priority for himself.' Directly supports 'acknowledged Legendre's book, and claimed the method anyway.' No overstatement.
Verbatim: 'This greatly hurt Legendre who fought for many years to have his priority recognised.' Supports 'Legendre spent years fighting for his name.'

Verbatim: 'The first clear and concise exposition of the method of least squares was published by Legendre in 1805.' Narration cites only 'published first' with no year, so it does not commit to 1805 vs the 1806 given elsewhere; the fact itself is accurately quoted.
Verbatim: 'In that work he claimed to have been in possession of the method of least squares since 1795.' Narration says 'since the seventeen nineties', which does not commit to 1795 vs 1794.

Confirmed in raw page: 'Gauss claimed in Theoria motus (1809) that he had been using it since 1794 or 1795.' (WebFetch summarizer missed it; raw HTML grep confirmed verbatim.) Narration 'seventeen nineties' straddles both datings without committing.
Verbatim: 'This naturally led to a priority dispute with Legendre.' Supports the dispute framing.

Verbatim: 'The technique is described as an algebraic procedure for fitting linear equations to data...' Sentence is about the method as Legendre published it; matches the two-parameter straight-line fit in the story rather than nonlinear orbit determination.

Verbatim: 'Geometrically, this is seen as the sum of the squared distances, parallel to the axis of the dependent variable, between each data point in the set and the corresponding point on the regression surface...' Supports 'Square every gap... and add them up.'

Verbatim: '...in 1822, Gauss was able to state that the least-squares approach... is optimal... errors have a mean of zero, are uncorrelated, normally distributed, and have equal variances, the best linear unbiased estimator... is the least-squares estimator.' Narration 'unbiased, equally noisy, independent, normal errors, nothing linear and unbiased beats it' tracks the source.

Confirmed in raw page: 'Gauss proved that the method has the lowest sampling variance within the class of linear unbiased estimators...' (WebFetch summarizer missed it; raw HTML grep confirmed verbatim.) Supports 'Gauss proved more.'
Verbatim: 'In general, an over-dimensioned system is obtained (for n > 4)...' Supports 'phone hears more satellites than it needs.'
Verbatim: '...which can be solved using the Least Squares adjustment.' Supports 'the standard fix is a least-squares adjustment.'
Verbatim: 'LINEST uses the method of least squares for determining the best fit for the data.' Supports 'Your spreadsheet's best-fit line is the same sum.'
